# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Clinical Update

### Introduction and Clinical Rationale
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia globally, carrying a significant burden of stroke and systemic thromboembolism [1, 2]. In patients with non-valvular AF (NVAF), more than 90% of stroke-inducing thrombi originate within the left atrial appendage (LAA) [3]. Standard stroke prevention relies on oral anticoagulation (OAC), which highly reduces ischemic event rates [4]. However, long-term OAC is limited by major bleeding risks, poor patient compliance, and absolute contraindications. This therapeutic gap motivated the development of percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) as a mechanical alternative for stroke prophylaxis [5, 6].

### Watchman Devices and Registries
The clinical development of percutaneous LAAC was pioneered by the WATCHMAN device (Boston Scientific). The PROTECT AF [7] and PREVAIL [8] randomized controlled trials demonstrated that LAA occlusion with the Watchman 2.5 device was non-inferior to warfarin for the composite endpoint of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death. A 5-year patient pool analysis confirmed long-term non-inferiority, showing a notable reduction in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality compared to warfarin [9]. Real-world registries, such as EWOLUTION, validated these outcomes in patient cohorts with elevated bleeding risks who were often unsuitable for OAC [10]. To address procedural limitations, the next-generation Watchman FLX was introduced, featuring a closed-end design and more anchors. Its safety and efficacy were demonstrated in the PINNACLE FLX trial [11], which showed low complication rates and excellent sealing. These findings have been supported by large-scale clinical registries, demonstrating the superior performance of the FLX over the older 2.5 model in routine clinical practice [12].

### Alternative Occlusion and Suture Systems
The Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott) represents another widely adopted occlusion system. It employs a dual-seal design (a lobe and a disc) that completely covers the LAA ostium. Observational registries reported high implant success and effective LAA closure with the Amulet [13, 14]. The landmark Amulet IDE trial directly compared the Amulet to the Watchman 2.5 device, proving non-inferiority for stroke prevention and showing a lower incidence of residual peri-device leaks [15]. In addition to endovascular plugs, epicardial suture-ligation devices, such as the LARIAT system, have been developed to achieve exclusion without leaving an intracardiac device [16, 17].

### Mechanical Closure vs. Anticoagulants
With the emergence of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) as first-line therapy for NVAF, trials have compared LAAC directly with DOACs. The PRAGUE-17 trial, which randomized high-risk AF patients to LAAC or DOACs, demonstrated that percutaneous closure was non-inferior to DOAC therapy regarding major cardiovascular and neurological events [18], a benefit that remained consistent at 4-year follow-up [19]. More recently, the ADVENT trial demonstrated that percutaneous LAAC with the Watchman FLX device was non-inferior to DOACs for both efficacy and safety endpoints, providing robust support for mechanical closure as a viable option in patients eligible for long-term OAC [20].

### Imaging and Post-Procedural Management
Successful percutaneous LAAC requires meticulous pre-procedural planning and intra-procedural guidance [21]. Multi-detector cardiac computed tomography (CT) is widely used to assess LAA morphology, ostial dimensions, and to rule out pre-existing thrombi [22]. Intra-procedurally, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has traditionally been the gold standard for guiding transseptal puncture and device sizing; however, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has increasingly emerged as a safe and effective alternative, reducing the need for general anesthesia [23]. Post-procedural antithrombotic regimens vary depending on individual bleeding risk and device type [24, 25]. Traditionally, Watchman implants required short-term warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) and aspirin monotherapy, whereas the Amulet and newer FLX protocols often employ DAPT or brief DOAC courses post-implantation [24].

### Complications and Procedural Challenges
Despite high technical success rates, LAAC is associated with unique complications. Device-related thrombus (DRT) is a significant concern, occurring in 2% to 4% of patients and correlating with an elevated risk of stroke [26, 27]. Peri-device leaks (PDLs), defined as residual patency around the device, can also occur; while minor leaks (<5 mm) were historically considered benign, recent data suggest that even minor PDLs are associated with an increased long-term risk of thromboembolism [28]. Other procedural complications, such as pericardial effusion or tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access issues, have drastically decreased with operator experience and improved technology [29].

### Future Horizons and Guidelines
Current guidelines assign a Class IIb recommendation to LAAC for patients with AF who have contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation [1, 2]. However, as technology improves and operator expertise grows, the indications for LAAC are expanding. Future clinical paradigms include combining LAAC with catheter ablation for AF in a single-stage procedure [30]. Ongoing randomized trials will continue to define whether LAAC can be utilized as a first-line therapy for stroke prevention across broader patient populations [29].
